title: The surviving witnesses
premise: Meet the surviving physical witnesses to biblical texts: what each preserves, how it is dated, where it has been, and what it can tell us.
intendedOutcomes: Distinguish an original composition from a surviving copy.
Read a manuscript identifier and find a trustworthy catalogue record.
Distinguish surviving coverage from reconstructed original contents.
Understand why date, completeness, language and textual value are separate dimensions.
Recognize Jewish custodianship of Hebrew texts and the multilingual history of Christian copying.
Describe a manuscript without claiming it proves more than it contains.

include: Copy dates and methods of dating
Coverage, loss, corrections, format and provenance
Selected translation witnesses as physical manuscripts
People, catalogues, editions and digitization that make witnesses accessible

defer.02: Detailed adjudication of individual variant readings
defer.03: Full Dead Sea Scrolls discovery history and non-biblical literature

boundaries.design: Deferred until all 25 content dossiers have completed their first pass.

contentSections.title: What is a witness?
substance: Define manuscript, fragment, scroll, codex, leaf, page, recto, verso, palimpsest, colophon and lectionary.
Separate the physical object, the literary work, the copyist’s text and a modern edited transcription.
Explain that a translation witness supplies a translated text, not automatically the exact wording of its source language.

contentSections.title: Before the great codices
substance: Introduce fragmentary survival and why different books have different surviving evidence.
Compare a small Gospel fragment with a substantial collection of letters.
Introduce papyrus as material and codex as format, rather than treating the two as synonyms.

contentSections.title: Large collections of Scripture
substance: Examine what the major Greek codices actually preserve.
Distinguish missing leaves from an intentional exclusion of a book.
Show why corrections, book order and associated writings are historical evidence.

contentSections.title: Hebrew texts and their custodians
substance: Connect ancient Hebrew witnesses with medieval Masoretic codices without presenting them as a single unchanged physical book.
Explain consonants, vocalization, accents and Masorah as distinct recorded features.
Respect separate Jewish and Samaritan transmission histories; select a documented Samaritan witness in the next verification round.

contentSections.title: Scripture across languages
substance: Introduce Greek, Hebrew, Latin, Syriac and Coptic witnesses.
Differentiate a translation’s proposed origin from the date of a surviving translated manuscript.
Include additional Armenian, Georgian and Ethiopic candidates without assigning dates before catalogue checks.

contentSections.title: Dates, journeys and survival
substance: Record dated colophons separately from palaeographic estimates.
Explain radiocarbon dating as evidence about material and calibrated ranges; do not equate it automatically to the writing date.
Distinguish excavated findspots, dealer reports, copying locations and modern repositories.
Compare missing pages, overwritten text, modern imaging and divided collections.

witnesses.title: Great Isaiah Scroll

date.label: Ancient Qumran witness; object-specific dating still to verify

witnesses.coverage: Isaiah; full chapter and damage inventory to ingest
witnesses.significance: An anchor for sustained Hebrew manuscript survival before medieval codices.
followUp: Verify date, exact extent, scribal hands and image permissions against the object record.

witnesses.title: Rylands Gospel fragment

date.label: Palaeographic dating disputed; retain attributed ranges

witnesses.coverage: Fragment of John; exact verse coverage to check against IGNTP transcription
witnesses.significance: A strong case for the difference between a surviving fragment and the complete work.
followUp: Import transcription and exact surviving verse portions.
Nongbri’s 2020 abstract argues that possible dates extend into the third century; read full argument and earlier dating studies before assigning a range.

witnesses.title: Chester Beatty Gospel and Acts papyrus

date.label: Date not normalized in this first pass

witnesses.coverage: Gospels and Acts collection; exact surviving portions pending
witnesses.significance: Pairs with P46 and P47 to avoid treating one manuscript as representative of the whole New Testament.
followUp: Read catalogue and Kenyon edition; verify date and surviving leaf inventory.

witnesses.title: Pauline letters codex
witnesses.shelfmark: P46; Chester Beatty BP II; Michigan inv. 6238

date.label: Third century in Michigan’s introductory guide

witnesses.coverage: Collection of letters, not the entire New Testament
witnesses.significance: The surviving codex is split between Dublin and Ann Arbor. Michigan describes 86 surviving leaves, with 30 there and 56 at Chester Beatty. Dealer acquisition limits archaeological context.
followUp: Separate reconstructed original contents and leaf count from surviving contents.

witnesses.title: Chester Beatty Revelation papyrus
witnesses.significance: Ensures the evidence set includes Revelation rather than only Gospels and Paul.
followUp: Read catalogue, date and surviving extent.

witnesses.title: Codex Sinaiticus
witnesses.coverage: Complete surviving New Testament; substantial but incomplete Old Testament; associated early Christian writings
witnesses.significance: The project identifies it as the earliest complete surviving New Testament. Its contents include Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas. Survival and book inclusion require separate explanations.
followUp: Import exact book coverage, shelfmarks and repository allocation; no claim that it is a complete surviving Old and New Testament.

witnesses.title: Codex Vaticanus
witnesses.coverage: Greek Bible; exact surviving original-hand coverage pending
witnesses.significance: Essential comparator for large Greek Bible collections. A verified digital object provides a route to primary images.
followUp: Extract original versus supplemental leaves and missing books.
Do not derive precise content or dating merely from the viewer shell.

witnesses.title: Codex Alexandrinus
witnesses.coverage: Greek Bible in four volumes; losses and associated Clement writings need explicit inventory
witnesses.significance: Connects substantial Greek biblical coverage with documented modern reception and scholarly printing.
followUp: Gather all four volume records; BL currently marks cited images unavailable.

witnesses.title: Codex Bezae
witnesses.coverage: Gospels and Acts, with a fragment of 3 John; incomplete
witnesses.significance: Facing Greek and Latin texts make it useful for language comparison; its distinctive readings need their own case studies.
followUp: Do not imply its Greek and Latin always match.
Check digital manuscript inventory before selecting leaves.

witnesses.title: Aleppo Codex
witnesses.coverage: Surviving portions of a formerly fuller Hebrew Bible
witnesses.significance: Introduces Masoretic annotation, communal custody and the difference between former and surviving completeness.
followUp: Acquire surviving-leaf inventory and precise dating source.
Separate Aleppo from the various Damascus Crowns.

witnesses.title: Leningrad Codex
witnesses.shelfmark: Commonly identified as B19a; verify normalized shelfmark

date.label: Early eleventh century; exact year unresolved in dossier

witnesses.coverage: Complete Hebrew Bible according to holding institution
witnesses.significance: A major complete Hebrew witness. The NLR page uses 1010; do not silently substitute commonly cited 1008/1009 without checking the colophon and scholarship.
followUp: Reconcile date conventions against the colophon and catalogue.
Verify relationship to modern edited Hebrew texts.

witnesses.title: Glazier Codex

date.label: Fifth century in Morgan conservation account

witnesses.coverage: Acts manuscript; precise surviving chapters pending catalogue
witnesses.significance: Broadens the witness set beyond Greek and introduces physical-book and binding research.
followUp: Confirm exact textual extent, dialect, date range and rights from catalogue.

witnesses.title: Codex Amiatinus

date.label: Date pending full custodial record reading

witnesses.coverage: Latin Bible; exact scope to verify
witnesses.significance: Candidate for a substantial Latin witness and its journey between northern Europe and Italy.
followUp: Read custodial exhibition document and manuscript record before promoting facts.

findings.claim: The Qumran collection includes biblical and non-biblical writings and predominantly fragmentary material.
The IAA describes both close resemblance to the Masoretic text and variation among biblical scrolls.
A manuscript’s modern ownership history may be much better documented than its ancient findspot.
The surviving copies differ substantially in physical extent; a fragment, a collection of letters and a complete New Testament are different kinds of evidence.
Modern transcriptions and imaging can improve access without changing the ancient age of the manuscript.
A copy made centuries later can preserve evidence about an earlier manuscript’s subsequently lost material.
findings.note: Use the Bezae recovery case after full reading, not as a general claim that every late copy preserves early readings.

researchQuestions: What is the earliest surviving evidence for each biblical book, under an explicit definition of evidence?
How much text survives in each witness, and what portion is physically missing?
What changes when a date is a range rather than a single year?
Which dates come from colophons, handwriting comparison, archaeological contexts or radiocarbon measurements?
What can versions and patristic citations establish, and how do they differ from direct manuscript evidence?
How have climate, collection history and publication shaped what survives and what is accessible?
How should two shelfmarks belonging to one codex be counted?
When can an absence be attributed to loss, and when is original omission demonstrable?

dataRequirements: Stable object ID, aliases and catalogue IDs
Format, leaves, dimensions and physical condition
Date as attributed proposals, range, method and source—not one forced number
Work and passage coverage with complete/partial/missing/reconstructed distinctions
Original hand, corrections and later supplements
Copy location, findspot, acquisition route and current repository as separate fields
Primary image or catalogue URL and access status
Source-linked claims, disputed fields and last checked date
Image and transcription reuse terms before publication
editorialRules: Do not quote a live manuscript total without a dated catalogue export and counting rule.
Do not call a fragment a complete book or a complete New Testament a complete Bible.
Do not treat all institutional summaries as equally precise; record contradictions.
Do not claim earliest always means best or number of copies alone settles a reading.
Do not confuse Hebrew, Greek, Latin or Syriac transmission with manuscript age.
Keep first-pass candidate entries visibly distinct from verified publication facts.
Preserve the site rule keeping Josephus-specific material in Scholars; none is needed for this dossier.
